blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The logic of hypothesis testing assumes that a specific claim about the population is true, then asks how unusual the observed data would be under that assumption. If the data would be very unusual, the claim is rejected; otherwise it is retained.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: The reasoning resembles proof by contradiction, or a court’s “innocent until proven guilty”. You assume a sceptical claim, for example “urban and rural children do not differ in mean weight”. You then ask: if that were true, how often would chance alone produce a difference as large as the one observed? If rarely, the claim becomes hard to believe. If often, you lack evidence against it. Lacking evidence against a claim is not the same as proving it.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Assume a new drug has no effect on recovery. If a difference in recovery as large as the one observed would arise by chance less than 5% of the time under that assumption, you have grounds to reject “no effect”. If such a difference would be common even with no effect, you do not reject “no effect”, although the drug may still have a smaller effect that this study could not detect.

points.html: The assumed claim is the null hypothesis (§8.2). How unusual the data are under it is measured by the p-value (§8.5), and the cut-off for “unusual enough” is the significance level (§8.4).
“Failing to reject” the claim is not “proving” it. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.
Every test in Chapters 9 and 10 (t-test, chi-square, ANOVA and the rest) applies this same reasoning to a different type of data.
